cards.statement: A disaster recovery plan that meets its data-loss target also meets its recovery-time target.
cards.explanation: RPO limits acceptable data loss; RTO limits recovery time. Meeting one target does not establish that the recovery design meets the other.
cards.misconception: Meeting the recovery point objective also establishes compliance with the recovery time objective.

cards.statement: Google's DR guide associates tighter recovery targets with higher application running costs.
cards.explanation: Tighter RTO and RPO targets often require more replication, capacity, and operational complexity, increasing the application's running cost.

cards.statement: A warm disaster recovery design keeps the application serving traffic throughout recovery.
cards.explanation: Warm DR includes an interruption while recovery resources are made ready. Prepared standby components reduce setup work, but the application still needs recovery time.
cards.misconception: Warm recovery keeps the application continuously available during recovery.

cards.statement: Google recommends an internal availability SLO that is stricter than the external SLA commitment.
cards.explanation: A stricter internal availability SLO warns the team early enough to address reliability problems before breaching the external SLA commitment.

cards.statement: Compute Engine resource-based commitments can follow a workload when it moves between regions.
cards.explanation: A resource-based Compute Engine commitment covers eligible usage in the region where it was purchased. Its regional scope stays fixed when a workload moves.
cards.misconception: A resource-based commitment transfers its discount coverage to another region with the workload.

source.title: Committed use discounts for Compute Engine

cards.statement: Compute flexible committed use discounts can reserve VM capacity for the committed workload.
cards.explanation: Compute flexible commitments discount eligible spend while capacity procurement stays separate. A workload needing assured VM capacity uses a reservation.
cards.misconception: Purchasing a compute flexible commitment also secures the workload's VM capacity.

source.title: Committed use discounts for Compute Engine

cards.statement: Rightsizing a VM reduces its compute bill by lowering the application's CPU utilization.
cards.explanation: Compute Engine charges for the chosen VM resources. Rightsizing changes the allocation; using less CPU inside an unchanged VM does not reduce its compute charge.
cards.misconception: Rightsizing saves money by lowering measured CPU use rather than changing allocated resources.

source.title: Apply machine type recommendations to VM instances

cards.statement: Pub/Sub lets billing and audit services receive the same events through independent subscriptions.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub delivers a topic's events independently to its subscriptions, so each business consumer processes its own copy.

cards.statement: Apigee can expose a JSON API to consumers while the backend continues to exchange XML messages.
cards.explanation: Apigee's mediation policies translate payloads at the API facade, allowing a legacy XML backend to serve JSON clients.

cards.statement: DORA counts a production release needing an immediate hotfix toward its change fail rate.
cards.explanation: DORA includes releases requiring urgent remediation, such as a hotfix, in the change fail rate. The metric tracks deployment instability.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework's AI and ML perspective applies its recommendations across pillars.
cards.explanation: AI and ML is a perspective that adapts recommendations from the framework's pillars to AI and ML workloads.

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework recommends shedding excess requests at the frontend during overload.
cards.explanation: The reliability pillar recommends shedding excess requests at the frontend so overload does less damage to backend components.

cards.statement: The regional deployment archetype automatically fails over applications to another region during a region outage.
cards.explanation: A regional deployment uses zones within one region. A region outage causes downtime, so recovery in another region needs a separately planned deployment or restore.
cards.misconception: A regional architecture includes recovery from a whole-region outage.

cards.statement: Google recommends extra capacity in multi-zone regional managed instance groups to sustain load during a zone outage.
cards.explanation: Google recommends sizing a regional managed instance group so its surviving zones meet the workload's capacity requirement after a zone fails.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL high availability places its standby instance in a different region from the primary.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL high availability places the primary and standby in different zones of the same region. This protects against a zonal failure.
cards.misconception: Cloud SQL high availability provides a cross-region standby.

cards.statement: Spanner automatically moves leaders to another read-write region when a multi-region leader region fails.
cards.explanation: If a multi-region configuration's default leader region becomes unavailable, Spanner places its database leaders in the second read-write region.

cards.statement: Standard Tier prioritizes keeping outbound traffic on Google's backbone until it reaches an edge near the user.
cards.explanation: Standard Tier normally exits Google's network near the resource's region. Peering or transit networks carry traffic onward to the internet user.
cards.misconception: Standard Tier prioritizes a long outbound path across Google's global network.

cards.statement: Cloud CDN can cache eligible content behind a global external Application Load Balancer.
cards.explanation: Cloud CDN integrates with the global external Application Load Balancer, letting eligible origin responses enter its edge cache.

cards.statement: Project Owners can delete Backup and DR backups during a backup vault's enforced retention period.
cards.explanation: Backup and DR blocks manual deletion of protected backups until enforced retention expires, even for a Project Owner.
cards.misconception: Project Owner permissions override a backup vault's enforced retention.

source.title: Backup vaults for immutable and indelible backups

cards.statement: Cloud Run preserves session files in an instance's local writable filesystem when it replaces that instance.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run loses files in the instance's local writable filesystem when that instance stops. Session data needing persistence belongs in external storage.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run carries instance-local session files into replacement instances.

cards.statement: Shared VPC lets network teams centralize subnet control while application teams use separate projects.
cards.explanation: Shared VPC keeps subnet administration centralized while workload teams administer resources in their separate projects.

cards.statement: A Private Service Connect endpoint lets consumers access producer VM subnets through private network routes.
cards.explanation: Private Service Connect endpoints expose a published service IP with NAT to its load balancer. They provide service access rather than general VPC connectivity.
cards.misconception: A Private Service Connect endpoint opens routed access to the producer's VM network.

cards.statement: A proxy Network Load Balancer preserves client source IPs in packets received by backend VMs.
cards.explanation: A proxy Network Load Balancer terminates the client connection and opens a backend connection. Source IP preservation in backend packets calls for a passthrough design.
cards.misconception: A proxy load balancer preserves the client's packet source address for the backend.

cards.statement: Dataflow lets a team reuse Apache Beam transforms across its batch and streaming pipelines.
cards.explanation: Dataflow uses Apache Beam's shared programming model for batch and streaming, allowing teams to reuse processing logic across those workloads.

cards.statement: Filestore supports concurrent access with POSIX file semantics for applications sharing files across VMs.
cards.explanation: Filestore provides POSIX compliance and concurrent file system access, which matters when multiple application instances share files.

cards.statement: Bigtable supports multi-row atomic transactions for applications that update related records together.
cards.explanation: Bigtable's atomic transaction boundary is a single row. An application that needs related changes across rows as one transaction needs another database design.
cards.misconception: Bigtable can commit several related rows as one atomic transaction.

cards.statement: Firestore's Android client synchronizes offline document updates by default when connectivity returns.
cards.explanation: Firestore's Android client enables offline persistence by default and syncs local document changes to the backend when the device reconnects.

cards.statement: Cloud Run supports privileged containers for applications that need host-level device access.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run excludes privileged containers from its runtime contract. Applications that depend on privileged execution need a different compute design.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run accepts privileged containers for host-dependent applications.

cards.statement: Compute Engine extended memory adds RAM to supported custom VMs while leaving the vCPU count unchanged.
cards.explanation: Supported Compute Engine custom machine series offer extended memory, letting memory-heavy workloads add RAM beyond the default ratio for their vCPU count.

source.title: Create a VM with a custom machine type

cards.statement: Cloud Interconnect encrypts traffic by default for an on-premises link carrying sensitive data.
cards.explanation: Cloud Interconnect traffic uses no encryption by default. A design that needs encrypted transport adds an encryption mechanism.
cards.misconception: Cloud Interconnect's private physical path supplies encryption by default.

cards.statement: Migration Center can assess PostgreSQL databases as part of a Google Cloud migration inventory.
cards.explanation: Migration Center accepts PostgreSQL inventory and performance data for assessment, helping architects include database requirements in migration planning.

cards.statement: Migration Center derives network dependency reports from vSphere scans of the source environment.
cards.explanation: Migration Center collects network connection evidence through the discovery client's OS scans. A vSphere scan does not supply that evidence.
cards.misconception: Hypervisor discovery alone supplies the connection evidence needed for network dependency planning.

source.title: Generate and analyze network dependencies report

cards.statement: Migration Center bases TCO comparisons for an asset group on the team's chosen migration preferences.
cards.explanation: Migration Center compares alternative preferences for an asset group, so architects can examine how target choices change migration cost estimates.

cards.statement: A rehost migration includes splitting a monolith into independently deployable services.
cards.explanation: A rehost migration retains the workload's design apart from changes needed to run in the target. Splitting a monolith changes the architecture.
cards.misconception: Rehosting includes changing a monolithic application's service architecture.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

cards.statement: Google recommends zero-downtime migration for workloads that tolerate planned cutover outages.
cards.explanation: Google advises against creating a zero-downtime requirement where possible because it adds redundancy and coordination complexity.
cards.misconception: Google recommends eliminating cutover downtime even when the workload accepts a planned outage.

source.title: Best practices for validating a migration plan

cards.statement: Moving purchased on-premises software to a hosted SaaS equivalent is a repurchase migration.
cards.explanation: Repurchase switches from the purchased on-premises application to a SaaS equivalent instead of migrating its code into a new runtime.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started

cards.statement: License Mobility through Software Assurance lets architects bring Windows Server licenses to Compute Engine.
cards.explanation: Windows Server's operating-system license falls outside License Mobility through Software Assurance. Google documents separate eligibility checks for other BYOL rights.
cards.misconception: License Mobility through Software Assurance covers the Windows Server operating system.
cards.volatilityNote: Software licensing eligibility depends on Microsoft's current terms.

source.title: Microsoft licensing on Google Cloud FAQ

cards.statement: Google recommends first-mover workloads with few dependencies for teams new to Google Cloud migrations.
cards.explanation: Google's first-mover guidance favors few dependencies so teams learn migration patterns before coordinating complex workload groups.

source.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Assess and discover your workloads

cards.statement: The Well-Architected Framework recommends frequent small changes with fast feedback to accommodate change.
cards.explanation: The framework's design-for-change principle favors incremental delivery and rapid feedback so teams can keep adjusting their architecture.

cards.statement: Cloud DNS shortens existing resolver cache entries when an architect lowers a record's TTL before migration.
cards.explanation: A lower Cloud DNS TTL takes effect after the previous cached value expires. Plan that wait before the migration cutover.
cards.misconception: Changing the authoritative TTL immediately shortens the lifetime of records already cached by resolvers.
